## Executive summary

This report explores the relationship between students' academic backgrounds, self-reported proficiency, preferences for programming languages, and project interests using survey data collected from 49 students in PSTAT 197A. We focused on three main questions: whether programming language preference relates to domain interests, whether programming proficiency influences preference for R or Python, and whether students with higher proficiency in mathematics, statistics, and computing are more likely to prefer industry projects. Our results showed that students with no programming language preference tended to have a broader range of domain interests, while students who preferred Python generally reported higher programming proficiency than those who preferred R. We also found that students who rated themselves as advanced in all three subjects were slightly less likely to prefer industry projects, although this relationship was not statistically significant. Overall, our findings suggest some interesting patterns in student interests and preferences, but since the data comes from a small sample size and is self-reported the conclusions we can draw are limited.

## Data description

The dataset comes from the class survey conducted for the Data Science Capstone (PSTAT 197A) at the start of Fall 2026. The survey collected information about students' academic backgrounds, technical skills, and interests to better understand the experiences and preferences of students in the class.

- **Sample:** Our analysis included responses from 49 students enrolled in the course. Since the survey was limited to students in one class, the sample may not be representative of the broader student population.

- **Academic background:** Students provided information about their majors and academic backgrounds.

- **Self-reported proficiency:** Students rated their own proficiency in programming, mathematics, and statistics. These ratings reflect students' own perceptions of their abilities rather than standardized assessments.

- **Programming preferences:** Students indicated whether they preferred Python, R, or had no preference.

- **Domain and project interests:** Students selected domains they were interested in (ex: public health, biology, technology, and social sciences). They also indicated their preference for industry or research projects.

- **Data preparation:** The survey responses were organized into two cleaned datasets, `background-clean.csv` and `interest-clean.csv`.

## Useful tips (remove this section)

Due to the visual editor, most common needs for authoring can be met using menu items in the RStudio IDE. For a comprehensive guide to Quarto, see the [documentation](https://quarto.org/docs/guide/); consult the documentation for anything you can't sort out in the IDE.

### Code chunks

Insert code chunks using the *Insert* drop-down menu or `ctrl + alt + I` . By default in this document, codes will not be shown but results will. If you want to change this behavior, add the chunk option `echo: true` as below.

```{r}
#| echo: true
my_df <- tibble(animal = c('snake', 'gecko'),
                threatening = c(TRUE, FALSE))

my_df
```

Code chunks will be executed in order when the document is rendered, so packages should be loaded at the very beginning of the document

### Rendering tables in markdown

Several functions exist for converting dataframes to markdown tables for nice display. A simple one from the `knitr` package is `knitr::kable()` .

```{r}
my_df %>% knitr::kable()
```

### Figures

To include any figures not generated by code chunks, use *Insert \> Figure / Image* or `![CAPTION](path/file.ext)` .

Most of the time code chunks producing plots will render fine. However, to adjust sizing or alignment, use the chunk options `fig-width` and `fig-height` . Captions can be added with `fig-cap` .

```{r}
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-align: left
#| fig-cap: A terrible plot.

my_df %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = animal, y = threatening)) + 
  geom_col()
```
